subtitle: Per-symbol coverage of the C++ <chrono> header. CORE SHIPPED 2026-08-25: 28 of 38 catalogued symbol groups, across 21 granular headers plus the umbrella. Covers duration, time_point, the three clocks, both casts, the C++17 rounding set, is_clock and the literals. NOT COVERED and deliberately absent rather than approximated: the C++20 civil calendar, the utc/tai/gps/file clock family, time zones, and the <format> integration -- a partial calendar is worse than none, and the zone half needs tzdata, a deployment dependency rather than a coding problem. std::chrono is itself C++11, so there is no back-port win on the core types; what re_std adds there is one behaviour across compilers, including an HONEST steady_clock::is_steady on platforms without a monotonic source, where implementations otherwise differ. Where re_std IS ahead: floor/ceil/round/abs and is_clock and days/weeks/months/years back-ported to C++11, and the duration and time_point mutators constexpr from C++14 where std waited for C++17. ONE TRAP TO KNOW: days, months and years here are FIXED-LENGTH durations, so t + years(1) advances by the mean Gregorian year, not to the same date next year.
legend_blurb: <chrono> provides type-safe time arithmetic: durations carrying their unit in the type, clock-tagged time points, and conversions that refuse to truncate silently.

symbols.name: duration<Rep, Period>
symbols.notes: The tick count plus the compile-time length of one tick. The period is a re_std::ratio and lives entirely in the type system, so a duration is exactly as large as its representation -- the abstraction is free. THE IMPLICIT CONVERSION RULE IS THE HEART OF THE TYPE: a duration converts implicitly only when the conversion is EXACT (ratio_divide<Period2, period>::den == 1), so seconds to milliseconds is implicit and milliseconds to seconds requires an explicit duration_cast. Floating-point reps opt out via treat_as_floating_point. Default construction leaves the count UNINITIALISED, matching std -- that is what keeps duration trivially default constructible. The mutators are constexpr from C++14, where std waited for C++17 (P0505R0): RE_STD AHEAD OF STD.

symbols.name: duration_values<Rep>
symbols.notes: zero / min / max for a representation type, and the customisation point for a user-defined rep. NOT numeric_limits: min() here means the LOWEST value, so it routes through numeric_limits<Rep>::lowest(). Using min() would silently make every floating-point duration's lower bound a tiny POSITIVE number -- a bug that survives every integral test.

symbols.name: treat_as_floating_point<Rep>
symbols.notes: Governs whether a rep may convert implicitly between any two durations. Floating-point reps are exempt from the exactness rule because every conversion among them is already approximate. The customisation point for fixed-point or checked-arithmetic reps. The _v spelling is C++17 in std and C++14 here -- variable templates are the binding constraint.

symbols.name: duration_cast<ToDuration>
symbols.notes: The explicit, lossy conversion. TRUNCATES TOWARD ZERO, which is not rounding: duration_cast<seconds>(milliseconds(-1999)) is -1s, so the result is LATER than the input. That surprises people writing timeout arithmetic around negative offsets. Dispatches four ways on whether the conversion factor's num or den is 1 -- not micro-optimisation: the identity cases can OVERFLOW if forced through the common type just to multiply by 1. The arithmetic type is common_type<ToRep, Rep, intmax_t>; without intmax_t in that set a conversion between two narrow reps would multiply in a narrow type and overflow. NOT PROTECTED: overflow of the common type itself (duration_cast<nanoseconds> of a large hours value). std requires no diagnostic and re_std adds none -- the check would cost every conversion and needs an error channel the interface has no room for.

symbols.name: common_type<duration, duration>
symbols.notes: The period is gcd(numerators) / lcm(denominators), and the order is not a typo: a SMALLER period is a finer tick, and only a finer tick represents both inputs without loss. The lcm is computed as (a / gcd) * b, never a * b / gcd -- the two are equal in exact arithmetic and not in intmax_t, and multiplying first overflows silently for denominators as ordinary as 1000000000, producing a wrong period rather than an error. Reuses internal::ratio_gcd from <ratio>, which is why <ratio> had to ship first.

symbols.name: duration operator+ - * / % (mixed periods and scalars)
symbols.notes: Mixed-period arithmetic converts both operands to the common type first, so nothing truncates. DIVIDING TWO DURATIONS YIELDS A NUMBER, not a duration -- dimensional analysis working correctly. The scalar operator/ and operator% must be constrained on !is_duration<Rep2> or they would win against the dimensional overload for `d / d` and silently return a duration. Multiplication is offered both ways round (d * 3 and 3 * d); `3 / d` is not, since a number over a duration is a frequency and this library has no type for it.

symbols.name: duration operator== != < <= > >=
symbols.notes: Both sides convert to the common period first, so seconds(1) == milliseconds(1000) is TRUE -- the question asked is 'same length of time', which is what keeps == consistent with the arithmetic operators. Only == and < carry logic. Shipped explicitly on EVERY tier including C++20, where std synthesises them from operator<=>: on C++11-C++17 they are the only way to compare, and on C++20 a non-rewritten candidate is preferred over a rewritten one, so they coexist with the three-way overload without ambiguity. Same choice as array and tuple.

symbols.name: duration operator<=>
symbols.notes: Delegates to the representation's own three-way comparison, so the category is strong_ordering for integral reps and partial_ordering for floating-point ones -- correctly, since a NaN count is unordered. NO synth-three-way fallback: a rep without operator<=> is a substitution failure at the trailing return type, so the overload drops out rather than silently getting a different ordering. Same simplification as tuple and array.

symbols.name: days / weeks / months / years
symbols.notes: BACK-PORT, nine years: each is a ratio typedef needing nothing C++20 supplies. MONTHS AND YEARS ARE AVERAGES: years is the mean Gregorian year, 31556952 seconds (365.2425 days), and months is exactly years/12. Neither knows about leap days, so `t + years(1)` does NOT give the same date next year -- that needs year_month_day, which is not implemented. days and weeks ARE exact, because a day is defined as exactly 86400 seconds, which sidesteps leap seconds by not modelling them.

symbols.name: floor<ToDuration> (duration and time_point)
symbols.notes: BACK-PORT, six years. Rounds toward NEGATIVE INFINITY without exception, which is what duration_cast should have been for most uses: floor<seconds>(milliseconds(-1999)) is -2s where duration_cast gives -1s. The cast's discontinuity at zero shows up as a one-unit error in exactly the region a test with positive fixtures never covers. Constexpr from C++11 via internal helpers, since relaxed constexpr bodies are C++14.

symbols.name: round<ToDuration> (duration and time_point)
symbols.notes: BACK-PORT, six years. Nearest, with TIES TO EVEN, not away from zero: round<seconds> of both 1500ms and 2500ms is 2s. That is what [time.duration.cast] specifies, and the reason is statistical -- always rounding halves up biases a long series upward, which accumulates into visible drift in timestamp aggregation. Excluded for floating-point target reps by SFINAE: the tie test compares two distances for exact equality, which a floating-point count cannot answer reliably.

symbols.name: time_point<Clock, Duration>
symbols.notes: A duration measured from a clock's epoch, TAGGED WITH THE CLOCK. That tag is the single most valuable thing the class does: a system_clock reading and a steady_clock reading are both offsets from an origin, but the origins are unrelated, so subtracting them would produce a plausible-looking duration that means nothing. Carrying the clock in the type makes it a compile error instead. Default construction IS the epoch -- the opposite of duration, deliberately, since a time_point has an obvious distinguished value and a duration does not. Mutators constexpr from C++14: RE_STD AHEAD OF STD (C++17).

symbols.name: system_clock (+ to_time_t / from_time_t)
symbols.notes: The wall clock. Its epoch is the Unix epoch -- a C++20 requirement that every implementation had already adopted, and which re_std guarantees at EVERY tier, so to_time_t and from_time_t are exact on both sides. NOT STEADY, and is_steady says so: NTP corrections, manual changes and DST transitions all move it, backwards included, so two successive now() calls can return a DECREASING pair. THE TIME SOURCE IS NECESSARILY PLATFORM CODE -- the only such code in the module, because the current time exists outside the program. Three compile-time tiers, best first: POSIX clock_gettime(CLOCK_REALTIME), C++17 std::timespec_get(TIME_UTC), then std::time at ONE-SECOND resolution. Tier 3 is the honest floor for pre-C++17 non-POSIX (older MSVC); QueryPerformanceCounter would do better but needs <windows.h>, which re_std will not pull into every TU that wants a duration. D_RE_STD_CLOCK_SOURCE reports which compiled in, and a forced-but-unsupportable choice is DEMOTED rather than allowed to error. Precision is microseconds regardless of source: int64 nanoseconds since 1970 runs out in 2262, and a wall clock that cannot represent the next three centuries is the worse trade.

symbols.name: steady_clock
symbols.notes: The interval clock: never jumps, never runs backwards. Its epoch is unspecified, so a single reading means nothing and there is deliberately no to_time_t and no conversion to system_clock -- a steady reading cannot become a date, and an interface that appeared to do so would be lying. is_steady IS COMPUTED, NOT ASSERTED: where no monotonic source exists the class falls back to the wall clock and is_steady becomes FALSE. Reporting false is the design decision -- claiming steadiness while reading a clock that jumps would let a caller's assert(end >= start) hold in testing and fail in production during a leap-second smear. The fallback is reached only on non-POSIX below C++17; CLOCK_MONOTONIC covers every Unix.

symbols.name: high_resolution_clock
symbols.notes: The standard permits this to be an alias for either clock or a distinct type, and implementations DISAGREE -- libstdc++ makes it system_clock, libc++ makes it steady_clock. That divergence is what re_std exists to remove, so one rule is fixed: steady_clock where a monotonic source exists, system_clock otherwise. IT IS A TYPEDEF, which is observable -- high_resolution_clock::time_point and steady_clock::time_point are the SAME type on most platforms, so code overloading on them will not behave as intended. Since the standard allows exactly this aliasing, such code was never portable. Prefer naming the clock you mean: the name promises resolution, the least useful of the three properties.

symbols.name: is_clock<T> / is_clock_v<T>
symbols.notes: BACK-PORT, nine years -- needs only void_t and partial specialisation, both C++11. symbols.notes: BACK-PORT, three years. Do not add any of those directives at namespace scope in a header -- `s` is a name other libraries want.
